_comment: Configuration and provenance for the KISS/DRY panel on the dashboard.
REPORTED, NEVER GATED. No threshold here fails a build. The suite's job is
argus's consumer contract; a red build has to mean argus broke, not that a
shell function grew. Gating a cleanliness number also invites Goodhart --
the number improves and the code does not -- and this repo already takes
that position about its own weights in failure-classes.json.
TWO TARGETS, REPORTED SEPARATELY. 'suite' is this repository: the
workflows, the tuple tables, the dashboard script. 'argus' is the package
under test. They are never summed. A combined score would let tidy tests
offset untidy source, and it would also let this board make a claim about
argus's internals that its maintainers have not agreed to -- the concern
failure-classes.json already raises about labelling.
ON THE EVIDENCE. Most of the classical cleanliness canon is weaker than
its reputation and is deliberately excluded. Cyclomatic complexity
correlates around 0.9 with raw SLOC, so it largely re-measures size;
Halstead's metrics and the Maintainability Index have no dependable
independent predictive value. What is kept below is what survived:
duplication  - Juergens et al. found it is not clones as such that hurt
but INCONSISTENT CHANGES to them, which are a real and
frequent defect source. This is the honest case for DRY.
cognitive    - Cognitive Complexity was validated against measured
comprehension time rather than against defect counts,
which is what 'simple' is actually supposed to mean.
tuple_dupes  - Local, and the best-evidenced of the three FOR THIS REPO:
PR #13 cut six tests because R12 was byte-identical to R7
and C11-C13 restated C10. Found by hand. The suite's tests
are parameter tables, so exact and near-duplicate rows are
computable. A redundant test also inflates the
denominator of the dashboard grade, so this one is not
only a style question.
Chidamber & Kemerer is validated but object-oriented, and this repository
is YAML and bash; it is not applicable and is not approximated.

suite.label: argus-test (this suite)
suite.note: Workflows, composite actions and the dashboard generator.

argus.label: argus (under test)
argus.note: The Python package, checked out at the ref under test. Reported for context; argus runs its own lint and coverage in its own CI, and this panel does not attempt to replace either.

duplication.label: Duplicated lines
duplication.what: Share of lines inside clone groups of at least the minimum size, found by token-based detection.
duplication.caveat: Type-1 and Type-2 clones only. Restructured duplication that says the same thing in a different shape is invisible to this, so a low number is weaker evidence than a high number.

cognitive.label: Cognitive complexity, worst unit
cognitive.what: Highest per-function score, plus how many units exceed the advisory level. Nesting costs more than branching, which is where it departs from cyclomatic complexity.
cognitive.caveat: Advisory level 15 follows SonarSource's default. It is a convention, not a finding.

tuple_dupes.label: Duplicate test tuples
tuple_dupes.what: Matrix rows whose parameters are identical once the id and display name are removed. Two rows that differ only by name are one test billed twice.
tuple_dupes.caveat: A deliberate duplicate is legitimate -- the suite keeps a knowingly-wrong control so the harness can be shown to go red. Annotate those in the workflow rather than deleting the check.

references.ieee: E. Juergens, F. Deissenboeck, B. Hummel, and S. Wagner, “Do code clones matter?,” in Proc. 31st Int. Conf. Software Engineering (ICSE), 2009, pp. 485–495.
references.note: inconsistent changes to clones are a measurable defect source -- the empirical basis for tracking duplication at all

references.ieee: M. Muñoz Barón, M. Wyrich, and S. Wagner, “An empirical validation of cognitive complexity as a measure of source code understandability,” in Proc. 14th ACM/IEEE Int. Symp. Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM), 2020.
references.note: correlates with measured comprehension time across ten studies; the reason Cognitive Complexity is here and Maintainability Index is not

references.ieee: G. J. Myers, “An extension to the cyclomatic measure of program complexity,” ACM SIGPLAN Notices, vol. 12, no. 10, pp. 61–64, 1977; and T. J. McCabe, “A complexity measure,” IEEE Trans. Softw. Eng., vol. SE-2, no. 4, pp. 308–320, 1976.
references.note: the original cyclomatic measure, recorded for provenance -- it is reported as context alongside cognitive complexity, not as the headline

references.ieee: J. Graylin, J. E. Hale, R. K. Smith, H. David, N. A. Kraft, and C. Ward, “Cyclomatic complexity and lines of code: empirical evidence of a stable linear relationship,” J. Software Engineering and Applications, vol. 2, no. 3, pp. 137–143, 2009.
references.note: the ~0.9 correlation with SLOC -- why cyclomatic complexity is not treated here as independent evidence of anything

references.ieee: M. Shepperd, “A critique of cyclomatic complexity as a software metric,” Software Engineering Journal, vol. 3, no. 2, pp. 30–36, 1988.
references.note: the standing methodological objection, predating the correlation studies that confirmed it

references.ieee: K. D. Welker, “The software maintainability index revisited,” CrossTalk, vol. 14, pp. 18–21, Aug. 2001.
references.note: why Maintainability Index is excluded rather than merely de-emphasised
